subdomainName: Understand and Integrate Security in the SDLC
title: SDLC models compared
prompt: Contrast Waterfall, Spiral, Agile and DevSecOps.
answerSummary: Waterfall: sequential phases, little room for change. Spiral: iterations with an explicit risk analysis in each loop. Agile: short sprints delivering working software and adapting to change. DevSecOps: integrates automated security testing into CI/CD and shifts security left.
examTrapWarning: The model known for risk analysis at every iteration is Spiral.

contrastData.ruleOfThumb: Spiral = risk-driven loops; DevSecOps = automated security in the pipeline.

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

subdomainName: Understand and Integrate Security in the SDLC
topicName: Security Gates at Requirements, Design, Coding, Testing, Deployment
title: Security activities at each SDLC phase
prompt: Order the SDLC phases and name the key security activity at each.
answerSummary: Requirements: security requirements and abuse cases. Design: threat modeling and architecture review. Development: secure coding, peer review, SAST. Testing: DAST, penetration testing, acceptance testing. Deployment and operations: change control, code signing, monitoring. Disposal: data sanitization and decommissioning.
examTrapWarning: Security is cheapest to add during requirements and design. Threat modeling belongs in design, not after deployment.

steps.label: Requirements
steps.detail: Define security and privacy requirements, abuse and misuse cases.

steps.label: Design
steps.detail: Threat modeling, secure architecture review, attack surface analysis.

steps.label: Development
steps.detail: Secure coding standards, peer code review, SAST, SCA.

steps.label: Testing
steps.detail: DAST, fuzzing, penetration testing, user acceptance testing.

steps.label: Deployment and operations
steps.detail: Change management, code signing, hardening, monitoring, patching.

steps.label: Disposal
steps.detail: Archive or sanitize data and retire the system securely.

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

subdomainName: Identify and Apply Security Controls in Development Environments
topicName: CI/CD Pipeline Security, Secrets Management, Environment Separation
title: Developers want real customer data for testing
prompt: The development team asks for a copy of the production customer database to reproduce a bug in the test environment. What is the right response?
answerSummary: Do not copy live PII into lower environments. Provide masked, anonymized or synthetic data, or reproduce the bug under production-level controls with data owner approval.
examTrapWarning: Test and dev environments usually have weaker controls and wider access, so copying production PII there creates a breach risk and may violate privacy law.

heuristicData.technicalReflexTrap: Copy the production database into test and rely on the developers to be careful.
heuristicData.managerAction: Keep environments separated: supply masked or synthetic data, and require data-owner approval with equivalent controls if real data is truly necessary.
heuristicData.governingPrinciple: Separate development, test and production, and protect sensitive data in every environment it lands in.

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

subdomainName: Identify and Apply Security Controls in Development Environments
topicName: CI/CD Pipeline Security, Secrets Management, Environment Separation
title: Securing the CI/CD pipeline
answerSummary: Keep secrets out of source code and inject them at runtime from a vault, sign build artifacts so tampering is detected, use least-privilege and ephemeral build runners, and protect branches with required reviews.
examTrapWarning: Deleting a secret in a later commit does not remove it from repository history; rotate any credential ever committed.
clozeTemplate: Pipelines should pull credentials from a {{c1::secrets vault::store}} instead of {{c2::hard-coding them in source::anti-pattern}}, {{c3::sign build artifacts::integrity control}} so tampering is detectable, and use ephemeral, least-privilege build runners. A committed secret must be {{c4::rotated::response}}.

subdomainName: Assess the Effectiveness of Software Security
topicName: Software Assurance Maturity Model (SAMM / BSIMM), Acceptance Testing
title: CMMI maturity levels
prompt: Order the five CMMI maturity levels.
answerSummary: 1 Initial (ad hoc) → 2 Managed (repeatable at project level) → 3 Defined (organization-wide standard processes) → 4 Quantitatively managed (measured) → 5 Optimizing (continuous improvement).
mnemonic: "I Must Define Quality Often": Initial, Managed, Defined, Quantitatively managed, Optimizing.
examTrapWarning: Level 4 is about measurement and statistical control; Level 5 is continuous process improvement.

steps.label: Initial
steps.detail: Unpredictable, ad hoc processes that depend on individuals.

steps.label: Managed (Repeatable)
steps.detail: Basic project management; processes can be repeated.

steps.label: Defined
steps.detail: Standard processes documented across the organization.

steps.label: Quantitatively managed
steps.detail: Processes measured and controlled with metrics.

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

subdomainName: Assess the Effectiveness of Software Security
topicName: Software Assurance Maturity Model (SAMM / BSIMM), Acceptance Testing
title: OWASP SAMM vs. BSIMM
answerSummary: OWASP SAMM is prescriptive and open: it tells you what to do across five business functions (governance, design, implementation, verification, operations) to raise maturity. BSIMM is descriptive: it reports what real organizations actually do, based on observation, so you can compare yourself with peers.
examTrapWarning: Prescriptive (SAMM) vs. descriptive (BSIMM) is the tested distinction.

subdomainName: Assess Security Impact of Acquired Software
topicName: COTS, SaaS, Open-Source Libraries, SBOM, Supply Chain Tampering
title: SBOM and source code escrow
prompt: Complete the acquired software risk controls.
answerSummary: An SBOM lists every component and dependency in a product so you can quickly check for affected versions when a new CVE appears. Source code escrow keeps the vendor's code with a third party, released to you if the vendor goes out of business or stops support.
examTrapWarning: Escrow protects against vendor failure, not against vulnerabilities. An SBOM gives visibility, not a fix.
clozeTemplate: A {{c1::software bill of materials (SBOM)::inventory}} lists all components and dependencies, enabling fast impact checks for new CVEs. {{c2::Source code escrow::arrangement}} protects the customer if the vendor {{c3::goes bankrupt or stops support::trigger}}.

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

subdomainName: Define and Apply Secure Coding Guidelines and Standards
topicName: OWASP Top 10 (Injection, Broken Access Control, SSRF, XSS, CSRF)
title: Web flaws and their primary fixes
prompt: For each common web vulnerability, give the primary defense.
answerSummary: SQL injection: parameterized queries / prepared statements. XSS: context-aware output encoding plus Content Security Policy. CSRF: anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies. SSRF: allow-list destinations and block internal metadata addresses. Broken access control: deny by default and enforce authorization server-side on every request.
examTrapWarning: Blacklisting characters or client-side validation alone is never the best fix for injection. Encoding output (not input filtering) is the main XSS defense.

rows: Parameterized queries / prepared statements; least-privilege DB accounts
Context-aware output encoding; Content Security Policy
Allow-list outbound destinations; block internal / metadata IPs
Deny by default; server-side authorization checks per request

references.source: OWASP Top 10 (2021) and OWASP Cheat Sheet Series

subdomainName: Define and Apply Secure Coding Guidelines and Standards
topicName: OWASP Top 10 (Injection, Broken Access Control, SSRF, XSS, CSRF)
title: Stored vs. reflected vs. DOM-based XSS
prompt: Contrast the three kinds of cross-site scripting.
answerSummary: Stored (persistent): the script is saved on the server (for example in a comment) and served to every viewer. Reflected: the script arrives in a request (often a crafted link) and is echoed back immediately. DOM-based: client-side JavaScript writes untrusted data into the page without the server ever reflecting it.
examTrapWarning: Stored XSS affects every visitor without them clicking a special link, so it usually has the widest impact.

contrastData.ruleOfThumb: Where the payload lives: server (stored), request (reflected), browser code (DOM).

columns.label: Reflected
points: Payload in URL or form input
Victim must follow a crafted link

references.source: OWASP Top 10 (2021) and OWASP Cheat Sheet Series

subdomainName: Define and Apply Secure Coding Guidelines and Standards
topicName: Buffer Overflows, Race Conditions (TOCTOU), Input Validation, API Security
title: Aggregation vs. inference (and polyinstantiation)
prompt: Distinguish database aggregation and inference attacks and name the classic countermeasure for inference.
answerSummary: Aggregation combines many individually low-sensitivity items into something more sensitive (troop counts per base reveal force strength). Inference deduces hidden information from what you can see (a missing record implies a secret). Polyinstantiation, query restriction and noise/perturbation counter inference.
examTrapWarning: Polyinstantiation (multiple records with the same key at different classification levels) is the textbook answer for inference.

contrastData.ruleOfThumb: Aggregation adds pieces up; inference reasons from them.

columns.label: Aggregation
points: Many low-level items form a high-level secret

columns.label: Inference
points: Deriving hidden facts from visible data
Also cell suppression, noise and perturbation

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

subdomainName: Define and Apply Secure Coding Guidelines and Standards
topicName: Buffer Overflows, Race Conditions (TOCTOU), Input Validation, API Security
title: ACID transaction properties
prompt: Define each ACID property for database transactions.
answerSummary: Atomicity: all of a transaction happens or none of it does. Consistency: transactions move the database from one valid state to another. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not interfere. Durability: committed changes survive failures.
examTrapWarning: Atomicity is about all-or-nothing; isolation is about concurrency. These are often swapped in distractors.

rows: All-or-nothing: partial transactions are rolled back
Each transaction preserves database rules and integrity
Concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

subdomainName: Define and Apply Secure Coding Guidelines and Standards
topicName: Buffer Overflows, Race Conditions (TOCTOU), Input Validation, API Security
title: TOCTOU race conditions
prompt: Complete the description of a time-of-check to time-of-use flaw.
answerSummary: A TOCTOU flaw happens when a program checks a resource (permissions, file identity) and later uses it, and an attacker changes the resource in between. Fix with atomic operations, file locking or by operating on handles rather than names.
examTrapWarning: Adding more checks does not fix a race; the check and the use must be made atomic.
clozeTemplate: A {{c1::TOCTOU::flaw name}} race occurs when a program checks a resource and then uses it later, and an attacker {{c2::changes the resource between check and use::exploit}}. The fix is to make check and use {{c3::atomic (locking or handles)::remedy}}.

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)
references.section: Ch. 21: Malicious Code and Application Attacks

subdomainName: Define and Apply Secure Coding Guidelines and Standards
topicName: Buffer Overflows, Race Conditions (TOCTOU), Input Validation, API Security
title: Buffer overflow defenses
prompt: Name the main buffer overflow defenses and what each one does.
answerSummary: Bounds checking and memory-safe languages prevent the overflow. Stack canaries detect a smashed stack before a function returns. DEP/NX marks data memory non-executable. ASLR randomizes memory addresses so jumps to injected code or gadgets fail.
examTrapWarning: ASLR and DEP make exploitation harder but do not remove the bug; input validation and bounds checking are the root-cause fix.

rows: Prevents writing past the buffer (root-cause fix)
Rust, Go, Java, C# manage memory bounds automatically
Detects overwritten return address before it is used
Data regions cannot execute injected code
Randomizes addresses so exploits cannot predict targets
